decision.reason: Inspecting McLaren et al. (2019; 10.7554/eLife.46923) alongside Yang et al. (2021) shows that McLaren et al. propose and test a stagewise multiplicative-bias model in which protocol- and taxon-specific bias is invariant in taxon ratios across sample compositions and can be calibrated using control communities. Yang et al. do not test multiplicative ratio invariance, stagewise bias partitioning, or calibration; instead, they fit uncalibrated linear regressions of input genomic DNA concentration on raw OTU read counts across evenness and tissue treatments (Methods 2.1.9; Results 3.2) and cite McLaren et al. (2019) as background mechanism (Section 1, p. 1149) and as 'the conventional wisdom that OTU size is a poor predictor of species relative abundances' (Discussion Section 4, p. 1157), in contrast to their explicit targeted replication of Elbrecht et al. (2017), which is already represented by shipped row 2328.

(2011; 10.1128/AEM.05220-11) empirically demonstrated in 1-step PCR that sample-identifying nucleotide barcodes on PCR primers induce template-dependent amplification bias and reduce community-profile reproducibility across technical replicates amplified with different barcodes versus the same barcode. Although Yang et al. (2021) do not test Berry et al.'s two-step PCR remedy and use arthropod COI mock communities on Illumina rather than 16S gut communities, they design and run a dedicated 1-step PCR 'Tag-bias test' (Section 1, p. 1149; Methods 2.1.9, p. 1152; Results 3.4 and Fig. 3, pp. 1153-1154) comparing community-ordination reproducibility (Procrustes correlations of Bray-Curtis NMDS ordinations) between technical replicates amplified with the same tags (n = 3) versus different tags (n = 12) across optimal, high-annealing-temperature, and touchdown PCR conditions, explicitly citing Berry et al. (2011) as a source of this tested hypothesis. This original is absent from shipped_rows (which contains only row 2328, Elbrecht et al., 2017).
